reference.source: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: The commonest cause of secondary parkinsonism, produced by dopamine-receptor-blocking or dopamine-depleting drugs, and a leading mimic of idiopathic Parkinson disease.
Classically more symmetrical than Parkinson disease, with bradykinesia and rigidity predominating; a symmetrical postural and action tremor may occur, though asymmetry does not exclude the diagnosis.
Onset typically within weeks to a few months of starting or increasing the offending drug, and it is potentially reversible after withdrawal, though recovery may take many months.

Common culprits include typical and atypical antipsychotics, the antiemetics metoclopramide and prochlorperazine, and dopamine-depleting agents; less-appreciated contributors include some calcium-channel blockers, valproate and certain antidepressants.
Persistent or progressive symptoms after drug withdrawal should raise suspicion of unmasked underlying Parkinson disease.
Coexisting tardive dyskinesia or orolingual dyskinesia alongside parkinsonism strongly favours a drug-induced aetiology.
Dopamine transporter (DaT) imaging is normal in pure drug-induced parkinsonism but abnormal where an underlying degenerative process has been unmasked, aiding difficult cases.

First-line management is identifying and stopping or substituting the causative agent; where an antipsychotic is essential, switching to a lower-liability agent (such as quetiapine or clozapine) is preferred, and antiparkinsonian drugs are generally reserved for refractory disability.
reference.pathophysiology: Drug-induced parkinsonism results from functional dopaminergic hypofunction in the nigrostriatal pathway. Dopamine-receptor antagonists (antipsychotics and antiemetics) block striatal postsynaptic D2 receptors, while dopamine-depleting agents reduce presynaptic dopamine availability; both shift the basal ganglia towards the parkinsonian state via overactivity of the indirect pathway and increased inhibitory output from the globus pallidus internus and substantia nigra pars reticulata. Non-dopaminergic mechanisms are implicated for some drugs such as calcium-channel blockers and valproate. Susceptibility increases with older age, higher potency and dose, and in some patients subclinical nigral degeneration lowers the threshold, such that the drug unmasks incipient Parkinson disease.
additionalDifferentials: atypical parkinsonian syndromes such as multiple system atrophy and progressive supranuclear palsy
hypothyroidism or depression with psychomotor slowing
additionalInvestigations: comprehensive medication review including antiemetics, calcium-channel blockers and antidepressants
dopamine transporter (DaT) SPECT imaging to distinguish reversible drug effect from underlying nigrostriatal degeneration
MRI brain to assess for vascular disease, hydrocephalus or atypical parkinsonian features
thyroid function tests and metabolic screen for treatable mimics
structured assessment for coexisting tardive dyskinesia and dystonia
monitored reassessment of parkinsonian signs over months after withdrawal of the offending drug
redFlags: markedly asymmetrical or rapidly progressive signs suggesting an underlying degenerative disorder
rigidity with fever, autonomic instability and altered consciousness indicating possible neuroleptic malignant syndrome
early falls, prominent autonomic failure or gaze palsy pointing to an atypical parkinsonian syndrome
failure to improve, or continued progression, after adequate withdrawal of the causative agent
reference.prognosis: Most patients improve after the offending drug is withdrawn, though resolution can take several months and a proportion have persistent deficits reflecting unmasked underlying Parkinson disease. Early recognition and drug cessation offer the best chance of full recovery.
pitfalls: assuming symmetry is required for the diagnosis and missing drug-induced parkinsonism when signs are asymmetrical
overlooking hidden culprits such as metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, flunarizine or cinnarizine
starting levodopa or dopamine agonists rather than removing the causative drug
expecting immediate resolution and prematurely concluding the drug was not responsible
failing to arrange DaT imaging or follow-up when symptoms persist, thereby missing unmasked Parkinson disease

management: Withdraw or reduce the offending dopamine-receptor-blocking or dopamine-depleting drug wherever possible, the definitive treatment, as symptoms are potentially reversible

Where an antipsychotic remains necessary, switch to a lower-risk agent such as quetiapine or clozapine, and replace metoclopramide or prochlorperazine with a non-dopaminergic antiemetic such as domperidone or ondansetron
Consider an anticholinergic or amantadine for symptomatic relief while awaiting resolution, weighing adverse effects in older patients
Reassess parkinsonian signs over the months following withdrawal, as recovery may be slow
Investigate persistent or progressive signs with dopamine-transporter (DaT) SPECT imaging and manage as idiopathic Parkinson disease if nigrostriatal degeneration has been unmasked
Refer to neurology where the diagnosis is uncertain or symptoms fail to resolve
